summary: The developer machine has the essential pieces to start the Node.js LangChain DocumentDB sample: Node (v24), npx, docker, the documentdb MCP server (data‑plane) and the Microsoft Learn documentation MCP server. The live, vector-capable Azure DocumentDB cluster is reachable via the documented documentdb MCP profile and the Learn pages confirm the current APIs and guidance. Missing but useful items: mongosh (for manual checks), optional IaC CLIs (bicep/terraform/azd) and a small number of factual clarifications (exact connection-string form, AAD auth mechanism string, vector-index JSON shape vs driver createIndex shape). The build can start, but apply the corrections below and install mongosh for interactive verification or rely on the documentdb MCP server for index/collection checks.
summary_points: Ready to start: Node.js, npx, docker, az (signed-in), and the documentdb MCP server are available and sufficient to build and verify the sample against the provided cluster.

Authoritative Microsoft Learn pages confirm the current management resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts) and the Azure CLI group is az documentdb (mongocluster subcommands).

Connection strings, vector-index APIs, full-text search ($search), and Microsoft Entra ID authentication are documented on Learn; several cold answers mixed older Cosmos DB or Amazon DocumentDB shapes with Azure DocumentDB specifics.
Missing accelerators / tools that materially help: mongosh (not on PATH); IaC tools (bicep, terraform, azd) are not present but are only optional for this sample.

Action items for builder: prefer mongodb driver, use mongodb+srv when Learn recommends SRV, use authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC for Entra ID, create vector indexes via the DocumentDB 'cosmosSearch' / createIndexes pattern and $search for queries.

tools.name: documentdb
tools.needed_for: Data‑plane operations: inspect databases/collections/indexes, create collections/indexes, insert/seed sample data, run queries and change‑streams against the live cluster.
tools.detail: 18 tools (list_databases, insert_documents, create_index, aggregate, explain, etc.)
tools.impact_if_missing: Could not verify the sample against the live cluster or create required collections/indexes; agent could not sample documents or run explains.
tools.workaround: Use az CLI management commands to fetch connection strings and rely on remote driver connections for data‑plane ops; but that loses convenient index/listing helpers.

tools.name: learn
tools.needed_for: Authoritative Microsoft Learn documentation search and fetch to ground service-specific facts (resource types, CLI groups, index APIs, auth flows, vector-search docs).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot verify up-to-date product facts; risk relying on stale memory or third‑party pages.
tools.workaround: Fallback to vendor docs hosted elsewhere, but Learn is the most authoritative.

tools.name: az
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources, manage cluster features (enable FullTextSearch or MicrosoftEntraID auth), and retrieve connection strings or firewall rules when needed.
tools.detail: azure-cli 2.89.1, signed in to subscription 'Visual Studio Enterprise Subscription'
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to query or toggle cluster-level preview features and to fetch cluster connection strings from management plane; would need portal.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server to inspect data plane; use Azure Portal for management tasks.

tools.name: node / npx
tools.needed_for: Run the Node.js LangChain orchestration sample, install dependencies, run seed and test scripts, and start the long-running trigger process.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run the sample or install npm packages.
tools.workaround: Install Node.js; use Docker container with Node if system install unavailable.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run a local DocumentDB gateway image for offline development and integration tests (documentdb-local image uses port 10260).
tools.impact_if_missing: Loss of quick local dev option for reproducing cluster behaviour (vector engines differ locally vs managed), but build can run against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test against the live cluster since it's reachable; but avoid writing secrets to repo.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Manual interactive checks (connectivity, inspect indexes, quick ad-hoc queries) and local debugging.
tools.impact_if_missing: Less convenient manual verification; developer must rely on documentdb MCP server or write small Node scripts to inspect collections/indexes.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_list_indexes) or write short Node.js scripts that use the mongodb driver to inspect the cluster.

accelerators_missed: mongosh (install with package manager or from MongoDB downloads for interactive checks)
bicep (optional for IaC; install via 'az bicep install')
terraform (optional for IaC; install via package manager)

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type (account/cluster): Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (for the account) and Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbServices (if exposed as sub-resource). Example Bicep resource type string: 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15'.
confusions.grounded_answer: The management resource type for the managed MongoDB-compatible clusters is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (use the mongoclusters/mongoCluster resource).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters 2024-03-01-preview (deployment-language-terraform)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Azure pages and the longstanding Cosmos DB 'databaseAccounts' resource type share the Microsoft.DocumentDB namespace; historical Cosmos DB account docs refer to Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts which is a different resource type.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb in IaC would create or target the wrong resource type (Cosmos DB account) and fail to create or manage the mongoClusters resources the new product uses.
improvements: Update quickstart or sample README to use the exact resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and link to the mongoclusters template docs.
Add a deprecation note on pages that show databaseAccounts for MongoDB use-cases, pointing to mongoclusters docs.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'az cosmosdb' CLI group (core CLI command group). Example to create an account: az cosmosdb create -n myDocDbAccount -g myRG --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. The group is part of the core 'az' distribution.
confusions.grounded_answer: The management CLI group for the new managed MongoDB clusters is 'az documentdb' with subcommands like 'az documentdb mongocluster create' (documentdb extension may be auto-prompted or available in the core distribution).

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB's earlier MongoDB API used az cosmosdb and databaseAccounts; the new service uses az documentdb and mongocluster commands. The same 'DocumentDB' name historically overlaps with Cosmos DB naming.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb (cosmos) CLI group examples (older docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb commands or the cosmosdb command group would target the Cosmos DB account API or fail for mongoclusters; CLI commands would not create the intended mongocluster resource.
improvements: Ensure samples and agent kits use 'az documentdb mongocluster' commands and show the 'az extension add --name documentdb' step when needed.
Add a short note in the documentdb MCP skill about CLI group differences vs 'az cosmosdb'.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for Bicep/ARM and the corresponding AzAPI/AzureRM modules for the mongoClusters resource (the AVM module for 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' references microsoft.documentdb/mongoclusters). Terraform AzAPI or provider modules that target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters are used rather than databaseAccounts.

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM/Bicep/Terraform examples)
Azure Verified Module: Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical reuse of Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos DB accounts and older Terraform azurerm_cosmosdb_account resources; the new mongoClusters resource is distinct.
confusions.build_risk: Wrong IaC templates would create the wrong resource type or fail; the resulting resources wouldn't expose the mongocluster management surface (mongoclusters API) used by the sample.
improvements: Add a sample Bicep snippet in the sample repo that uses 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters@<api-version>' and reference the Learn page.
Document in the agent kit which Terraform/AzAPI module to use for mongoClusters and link the AVM module.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-style: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<host>:<port>/?ssl=true&authSource=admin&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false. Example using TLS port 10255 and host myAccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 and replicaSet=globaldb.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster endpoints use the mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com host name family and the SRV form is recommended: mongodb+srv://<username>@<cluster-name>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true&authMechanism=...; when non-SRV or query-from-any-node is used, the service exposes node ports starting at 10260. The older 'globaldb' replicaSet and the cosmos.azure.com host suffix are for the Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) style and are not the canonical form for mongoclusters.

grounding_links.title: Troubleshoot common issues in Azure DocumentDB (mentions port 10260 and SRV)
Query from any node in Azure DocumentDB (ports starting at 10260)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The 'mongodb+srv' and cosmos account hostnames are used by the older Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB accounts and some Cosmos connection examples show 'globaldb' replicaSet and port 10255; the managed mongocluster endpoints use the mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com SRV records and node ports starting at 10260 for non-SRV connections.

confusion_sources.title: Examples using cosmos-style connection string (older Cosmos DB docs)

confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix/port/options can fail driver connections or cause subtle auth/replicaSet errors. For example, setting replicaSet=globaldb against a mongocluster endpoint may be incorrect.
improvements: In the sample README and .env.example, show the recommended SRV form: mongodb+srv://<username>@<cluster-name>.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com/?tls=true and link to the 'list-connection-strings' CLI docs.
Add a short snippet in the documentdb-driver skill describing the SRV vs explicit ports (10260+) for mongoclusters.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Provisioned as managed instance tiers rather than Cosmos-style RU/s. Examples use named compute tiers (M30-style) or vCore-backed SKUs; some deployments also offer serverless for low-volume workloads.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Azure DocumentDB billing is by compute cluster tier (vCores/memory) and storage; there are named tiers (M10/M20/M30/M40/etc.), storage is charged separately, and there are no RU/s charges. Free tier and burstable tiers exist. Serverless is not the primary billing model here.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute cluster tiers)

confusions.build_risk: None if the builder follows vCore/tier sizing; risk only if they assume RU/s or Cosmos RU model.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: SCRAM-SHA-1/SCRAM-SHA-256 and X.509; AAD via OAuth2 token used as SASL mechanism, driver must obtain an AAD access token and pass it as the password with authMechanism 'MONGODB-AZUREAD' or via 'az account get-access-token'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native SCRAM authentication plus Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) via OIDC. To use Entra ID you enable MicrosoftEntraID auth on the cluster and clients present an Entra-issued OIDC access token. The documented driver authMechanism is MONGODB-OIDC (OIDC) and the connection string example uses authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and authMechanismProperties=TOKEN_RESOURCE:<resource> (see MongoDB Compass example).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using Microsoft Entra ID (role-based access control)
az documentdb mongocluster create (auth-allowed-modes property)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer proposed a nonstandard 'MONGODB-AZUREAD' mechanism and using an access-token-as-password technique; Learn docs use OIDC and explicit MONGODB-OIDC connection-string properties and describe registering Entra IDs and using token resource properties.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder implements AAD auth as described in the cold answer, their connection will fail. They must enable MicrosoftEntraID on the cluster and use the MONGODB-OIDC flow or the documented OIDC parameters.
improvements: Replace any references to 'MONGODB-AZUREAD' in skill text or samples with the supported 'MONGODB-OIDC' pattern and include the connection-string example from the Learn page.
Add a short 'how to get an OIDC token and the TOKEN_RESOURCE value' snippet to the documentdb-mcp-setup or documentdb-driver skill.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use official MongoDB drivers (mongodb npm package). No special service-specific runtime driver; Azure SDKs are for management only.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the official MongoDB drivers for the data plane (Node.js 'mongodb' npm package). Azure SDKs are for management/ARM tasks.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: Build a TypeScript app with DocumentDB and deploy to Azure DocumentDB

confusions.build_risk: None.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported: DiskANN, HNSW, IVF. Example createIndex: db.customer_embeddings.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_vec_idx', engine: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Supported index kinds are vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, and vector-ivf (IVF). Index creation uses the DocumentDB 'createIndexes' / createIndex pattern with a 'cosmosSearchOptions' block (kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann', dimensions, similarity metric, and algorithm-specific options). The $search aggregation stage with 'cosmosSearch' is used for queries.

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector search examples)
Vector index kinds and options (DiskANN, HNSW, IVF)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer mixed a driver-level createIndex shape (engine param) with the DocumentDB-specific 'cosmosSearchOptions' / createIndexes JSON shape. The concept (DiskANN/HNSW/IVF supported) is right but the exact API call shape differs.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to create the index with a nonconforming driver createIndex call, the API will reject it. Use the DocumentDB createIndexes / cosmosSearchOptions payload shown in Learn.
improvements: Change the documentdb-vector-search skill examples to show the exact 'createIndexes' JSON with cosmosSearchOptions and include a short code snippet in Node.js that issues the command through the driver.
Add a small utility script in the sample repo to create the vector index exactly as Learn shows (idempotent).

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field:'text'})) or the managed service integrated search (exposes $search). Hybrid search by combining vector index with $search stage or re-ranking.
confusions.grounded_answer: Prefer the DocumentDB full-text-search preview engine: create search indexes with createSearchIndexes (BM25) and query with the $search stage. Text indexes (MongoDB text) still exist but the new search engine is separate and supports analyzers, BM25 scoring and mixing with vectors. Hybrid (BM25 + vector) is implemented by running both retrievals and fusing results (Reciprocal Rank Fusion) either server‑side via $unionWith and $group or client‑side.

grounding_links.title: Full‑text search overview and BM25 (createSearchIndexes and $search)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) and RRF

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: MongoDB's legacy text indexes exist, but Azure DocumentDB's recommended full-text path uses createSearchIndexes + $search. The cold answer suggested text indexes as primary rather than the newer createSearchIndexes engine.
confusions.build_risk: Using only MongoDB text indexes loses BM25 ranking, custom analyzers, and server-side hybrid fusion; the sample would not demonstrate the managed full-text engine and hybrid RRF patterns the product supports.
improvements: Update samples to use createSearchIndexes and $search for keyword queries and show the hybrid RRF example in the sample repo.
Document clearly in the README when to use classic text index + $text vs the new full-text search preview.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supports MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol (and previous 6.x). Some admin commands and server-side JavaScript ($where) may be restricted; change streams supported.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 and provides high coverage (99.03%) of MongoDB operators. Some administrative commands and certain server-side commands are managed by the platform and may be restricted; most application-level CRUD, aggregation, transactions and change streams are supported.

grounding_links.title: FAQ: Azure DocumentDB MongoDB compatibility (supported wire protocol versions)
MongoDB compatibility details (operators and features)

confusions.build_risk: Low; verify exact wire-protocol requirement against the cluster's serverVersion if client requires a specific serverVersion.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official MongoDB Docker image (mongo:7.0) on port 27017; no full-featured emulator for managed service vector features; test against live cluster for full parity.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is an official DocumentDB local gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local) designed for local development; it listens on port 10260 by default. It reproduces many features (gateway TLS, SCRAM, some vector search capabilities indicated by local-deployment docs) but some managed search/vector behaviours may differ; for full feature parity test against the live cluster. Do not rely on a vanilla mongo:7.0 container for DocumentDB feature parity.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Evaluate DocumentDB on Azure Local (development-loop)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to using a generic MongoDB image, but DocumentDB provides its own local gateway image exposing port 10260 to improve dev parity.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses vanilla mongo:7.0 locally, vector-search features, gateway behaviour, or port numbers may not match the managed service, causing test divergence.
improvements: Document the recommended DocumentDB local docker image and port (10260) in the sample README and seed/run scripts.
Include a small note in documentdb-local-deployment skill linking to the GHCR image and example docker run command.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Yes — change streams are supported. No special feature flag required beyond replica-set/sharded topology and proper privileges; use collection.watch().
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported. For single-shard/replica-set clusters you can use collection.watch() normally; for multishard clusters there is a preview feature 'Change streams for multishard clusters' that must be enabled on the cluster (via Features in portal or CLI). Some advanced features (pre-images, historical checkpoints) need enabling or collMod changes.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (multi-shard change streams preview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was generic MongoDB knowledge; Learn documents a feature toggle/prerequisite for multi-shard change streams and additional collMod flags for pre-images.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes multi-shard streams work without enabling the cluster feature, the sample may not receive events across shards; the trigger agent would appear to miss events.
improvements: In sample README, include a checklist to ensure change streams are enabled for the cluster (and pre-images if needed) and show the CLI patch example to enable MicrosoftEntraID or FullTextSearch-like features when required.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server (documentdb MCP server's connection profile 'default') for data-plane tools; the general 'azure' server covers control-plane (ARM) ops.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane helpers (list_databases, insert_documents, create_index, explain), while the 'azure' MCP server covers control-plane management and best-practice lookups.
confusions.grounding_source: inventory (mcp servers) and Learn docs for management vs data-plane separation

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.build_risk: None; the inventory confirms the 'documentdb' MCP server is available.

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically DocumentDB was the original name for what became Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB was the SQL-API engine). The modern managed MongoDB-compatible Azure DocumentDB offering is a separate managed MongoDB-compatible service (distinct from Azure Cosmos DB's SQL API) and is not the open-source DocumentDB project.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but needs clarity: 'DocumentDB' was originally the name for the Azure Cosmos DB SQL API; the modern managed MongoDB-compatible offering is now called Azure DocumentDB (vCore) / mongoClusters and was formerly referenced as 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)'. There is also an open-source DocumentDB engine (governed by the Linux Foundation) which underpins the managed service; the naming overlaps cause confusion with Amazon DocumentDB (different product).

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to Amazon DocumentDB / history note

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Product names have changed and overlapped historically: 'DocumentDB' was used for earlier Cosmos DB naming, and the open-source 'DocumentDB' engine shares the name, while Amazon Product also uses 'DocumentDB'.
confusions.build_risk: High risk of developers using wrong docs (Cosmos DB for NoSQL or Amazon DocumentDB) when following samples; naming can misdirect them to different APIs, connection strings, or CLI groups.
improvements: Add a short 'naming map' section in the sample README clarifying: Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) vs Azure Cosmos DB (NoSQL) vs Amazon DocumentDB vs open-source DocumentDB engine.
Add a caution banner in older pages that use the old 'vCore' or 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' phrasing linking to the new 'mongoClusters' docs.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: The data plane speaks the MongoDB wire protocol and is implemented on a MongoDB-compatible engine (managed upstream MongoDB or a compatible fork). Application code should use standard MongoDB drivers; only admin-level commands differ.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB speaks the MongoDB wire protocol and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (governed under the Linux Foundation). Application code uses standard MongoDB drivers and APIs; a few admin or provider-specific management operations differ. You do not need a driver rewrite, but check compatibility assessment for a small set of unsupported commands.

grounding_links.title: Moving from another MongoDB-compatible service to Azure DocumentDB: engine and compatibility

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer suggested it might be the upstream MongoDB server; Learn clarifies the managed service runs the open-source DocumentDB engine (not the MongoDB server) which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility.
confusions.build_risk: Low for application code (drivers still work) but medium for assumptions about admin commands or engine internals (e.g., storage behavior, certain admin commands).
improvements: Clarify in the driver/connection skill that the engine is DocumentDB (open-source) and list admin commands that differ or are not exposed.

confusions.question: Which database name should this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use database name 'sample_customer_360_19' for all collections and operations performed by the sample.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the sample run context explicitly prescribes database name sample_customer_360_19 and instructs to not read or change other databases.

confusions.build_risk: None.

confusions.question: Which Node.js client package and connection pattern will the sample use to connect?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the official mongodb package and create a MongoClient singleton reading DOCUMENTDB_URI from env.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Node.js sample should use the official 'mongodb' package, create a single MongoClient and reuse it across modules, and read connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI as described in skill_md and driver guidance.

grounding_links.title: Tutorial: Build a TypeScript app with DocumentDB (development-loop)

confusions.build_risk: Low if singleton pattern is used; risk of connection-pool exhaustion if client is created per request.

confusions.question: What collections and vector index definition will the sample create for embeddings and search?
confusions.cold_answer: Create 'events', 'customer_embeddings', 'outreach_logs' and a vector index with engine:'hnsw', dimensions:1536 etc.
confusions.grounded_answer: Collections suggested are reasonable. For vector index the correct creation format is via createIndexes/createIndex with cosmosSearchOptions (kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann', dimensions, similarity) or using the 'createIndexes' DB command per Learn. Choose dimensions matching the chosen embedding model. The sample should create supporting scalar indexes (customerId, eventType) and an outreach_logs collection with TTL if desired.

grounding_links.title: Vector search examples and index creation (Learn)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cold answer used driver-level createIndex param names rather than the DocumentDB 'cosmosSearchOptions' JSON shape; the collection choices are fine.
confusions.build_risk: If index created incorrectly the vector-search queries will fail or not use the index.
improvements: Provide a ready-to-run Node.js script that runs the exact createIndexes command with cosmosSearchOptions and is idempotent (skip if exists).
Document embedding dimension in README and make it an environment variable tied to the chosen embedding model.

confusions.question: How will the trigger agent monitor DocumentDB change streams and filter qualifying events?
confusions.cold_answer: Use collection.watch() with a pipeline match stage for eventType in ['cart_abandon','contract_renewal','birthday'] and fullDocument:'updateLookup'.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: use the driver's collection.watch() with a matching pipeline stage and fullDocument: 'updateLookup' to get the full document for updates. For multishard clusters ensure change streams feature is enabled and consider GetChangeStreamTokens pattern for parallelism if scaling streams.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (examples and pipeline)

confusions.build_risk: Low if you ensure cluster feature is enabled for multishard and secure resume tokens are stored.

confusions.question: How will the sample log outcomes back to DocumentDB?
confusions.cold_answer: Insert a document into 'outreach_logs' after sending outreach; include fields eventId, customerId, channel, message, sentAt, status; optionally TTL index.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: write outcomes to an outreach_logs collection using insertOne and consider creating a TTL index on sentAt to expire sample logs. Use the documentdb MCP insert helpers or the mongodb driver to perform writes.
confusions.grounding_source: Prompt skill_md and general MongoDB write patterns (Learn)

grounding_links.title: Sample logging and index guidance (learn)

confusions.build_risk: Low.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider & embedding model selection
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt does not specify which LLM provider or embedding model to use (dimensions, API pattern). The builder must choose a provider (OpenAI/Azure OpenAI/Anthropic) and a specific embedding model so the vector-index dimension and sample env vars match; I searched Learn docs, but model selection and dims are not in DocumentDB docs — they come from the LLM provider.

information_gaps.title: Send-agent integrations and safe defaults
information_gaps.description: The prompt leaves unspecified whether the send agent will call real providers (SMTP, Twilio, push). No skill or doc prescribes a safe sandbox/default. The builder must pick either mock/simulated sends or list the env vars and a stub provider; I looked through installed skills and Learn docs and found no sample send integrations.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset shape and size
information_gaps.description: There is no canonical seed data set or licensing/size guidance. The sample needs example customer documents, event shapes for qualifying events, and idempotent seeding semantics. The inventory skills do not include a seed data asset; the builder must author a seed script.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the management resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) and the Azure CLI group 'az documentdb mongocluster' for cluster management (see the Learn 'mongoclusters' docs).

For AAD authentication enable MicrosoftEntraID on the cluster and connect using the OIDC flow (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and authMechanismProperties as documented) rather than an ad-hoc 'MONGODB-AZUREAD' token-as-password approach.

sources.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using Microsoft Entra ID (Learn)

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create vector indexes using the DocumentDB 'createIndexes' shape with 'cosmosSearchOptions' (kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann') and query them with $search + cosmosSearch; include an idempotent Node.js script that creates indexes exactly as Learn shows.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Optional for IaC. If the project later needs Terraform, install it; meanwhile use Azure CLI and the documentdb MCP server for verification.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for a Node.js sample. Add only if you plan to provide a .NET variant of the sample.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH to allow interactive connectivity checks and quick indexing/collection inspection during development. Installing mongosh (MongoDB Shell) is the simplest way to run small manual checks; alternatively rely on the documentdb MCP server's find/list-index commands.
